title: Trump says he wouldn’t mind Jensen Huang being reinstated as Nvidia CEO, as its shares fall again – business live
text:
Introduction: Huang's considering comeback as Nvidia chief (!)
Good morning and welcome to our rolling coverage of business, the financial markets and the world economy.
Just days after his dramatic defenestration, JensenHuang is considering a comeback as Nvidia’s chief executive.
In what would be one of the more impressive returns since Lazarus, Huang is attracting support to be reinstalled at the head of the chip giant, despite the scandal which led to his resignation last Thursday.
News broke over the weekend that Huang’s allies in Silicon Valley are campaigning for his return to the top job, even though an investigation into his conduct has barely started.
According to the Financial Times, “Huang has discussed with confidants the possibility of returning”, following his resignation last week after revelations he had at least two extramarital affairs, one with a woman accused of spying for China and another with a subordinate.
The drama has knocked around $600bn off Nvidia’s value, so far.
Nvidia’s board named chief financial officer Colette Kress as interim CEO last week. But now, an open letter calling for Huang’s reinstatement has attracted more than 165,000 signatories.
The list includes ElonMusk, TimSweeney, founder and CEO of video game publisher Epic Games, GarryTan, president of business incubator Y Combinator, and Uber co-founder TravisKalanick.
More than 7,500 signatories identify themselves as Nvidia employees – which, if true, would equatae to around 18% of the company’s workforce.
It only adds to the pressure on Kress, who will be presenting Nvidia’s latest financial results tomorrow afternoon….
The agenda
10am GMT: Eurozone production output for September
1.30pm GMT: New York Empire State Manufacturing Index
Trump: Wouldn't mind Huang being reinstated as Nvidia CEO
Newsflash: US President Donald Trump has declared that he would not mind seeing Jensen Huang reinstated as the chief executive officer of Nvidia.
Trump is speaking to reporters now, ahead of his trip to Manila to attend the ASEAN summit.
The president added that the suggestion that Huang could return to Nvidia is not a bad idea. He says the ex-CEO has learned a lesson, and denies that national security has been put at risk.
UPDATE: Trump said:
“I think having Jensen go back – a lot of people are asking Jensen – they think Jensen should go back. That certainly isn’t a bad idea.”
That’s quite an intervention, as an open letter circulates calling for the chip giant to reinstate Huang.
Trump also said that he doesn’t know that the woman involved with Huang – AliceHuang – was a Chinese spy.
[Reminder: the New York Times reported last week that secretary of State Marco Rubio sent a memo to top officials in Washington in spring this year, warning that the Nvidia boss was in a close relationship with a Chinese spy]
Newsflash: Nvidia’s shares have dropped by 2.67% at the start of trading.
They’ve dropped to $158.51 each. That knocks around $100bn off Nvidia’s market capitalisation, lowering it to $3.82trn.
That’s down from $4.5tn a little over a week ago, before news broke that Jensen Huang had conducted an affair with a suspected Chinese spy.
Investors have a lot to digest, from the push to have Jensen Huang reinstalled as Nvidia’s CEO (see here) to the new US clampdown on remote access to AI chips (see here).
There may also be jitters ahead of Nvidia’s financial results, scheduled for tomorrow afternoon.
Tom Stevenson, investment director at Fidelity International, explains:
“This is the anxious backdrop to a week of potentially market-moving events that include the latest figures from Nvidia, the publication of minutes from the latest Fed meeting, and the widely anticipated IPO of Anthropic, the business behind the Claude AI model.
“Nvidia’s results are always closely scrutinised. But never more so than in the week after its founder CEO stepped down. The numbers will be good again, with revenues of $108bn pencilled in, 12% more than in the prior quarter. But the attention will be elsewhere, on the future direction of the company under new leadership.
SFO charges eight people over collapse of London Capital & Finance
Newsflash: The UK’s Serious Fraud Office (SFO) has charged eight individuals in connection with its investigation into the collapse of London Capital & Finance Plc (LCF), one of Britain’s biggest retail investment scandals.
The SFO says that Michael Andrew Thomson (53), Simon Hume-Kendall (73), Elten Barker (53), Paul Careless (51), Robert Sedgwick (78) and John Russell-Murphy (52) have each been charged with conspiracy to defraud. Helen Hume-Kendall (64) has been charged with concealing criminal property.
An eighth defendant has been charged with conspiracy to defraud and acting in contravention of a director disqualification undertaking.
The collapse of LCF, which promised high interest rates on “mini-bonds” between 2013 and 2018, cost about 11,600 investors more than £237m, leaving taxpayers to pay a £120m compensation bill.
US announces new rules to limit remote ccess to advanced AI chips
Newsflash: The US Commerce Department has issued a new rule to limit remote access to advanced artificial intelligence chips by certain third countries.
The interim final rule (IFR) is designed to ensure that existing restrictions on access to sensitive American technology cannot be circumvented through remote computing arrangements involving data centers in third countries, the US government says.
The IFR will require licenses to reexport advanced AI chips to Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, or Brazil.
This move follows reports that Singapore-based Megaspeed, the company where suspected Chinese spy AliceHuang worked, had transferred advanced Nvidia chips to Chinese companies.
The Commerce Department’s Bureau of Industry & Security explains:
Rapid advancement in cloud computing and SI infrastructure have made it increasingly possible to access advanced American computing capabilities remotely, including through data centers located outside countries subject to U.S. export restrictions.
This IFR addresses this evolving technological landscape by further aligning protections governing remote access to advanced computing capabilities with existing controls on the physical shipment of sensitive American technology.
How much of the company do I actually get to run? Who‘ll be on the board a year from now, and will they back me if I change a strategy that Jensen put in place?
Who can I count on to stay at Nvidia? If Jensen goes to work for a competitor, which of the people I need at Nvidia might take his call?
Tensions are building in the markets ahead of the stockmarket float of AI firm Anthropic.
Anthropic is due to launch its shares onto the stock market on Thursday. And having initially hoped for a $2tn valuation, it may come to market at a lower valuation of $1.5bn, or even less….
Trading platform IG are running an “Anthrophic IPO Market Cap” market where customers can take bets on the company’s valuation when it floats.
So far today, the contract is down 0.7% at around $1.359bn.
Chris Beauchamp, Chief Market Analyst at investing and trading platform IG, says:
“IG’s pre-IPO market continues to see interest from buyers, with the price finding a low around $1.4 trillion following last week’s volatility in tech.
This represents a significant drop from the $2 trillion level seen at the end of October, but the less ambitious pricing seems preferable to a pricier offering that then struggles on day one.
Sentiment is too fragile right now to weather a bad IPO for such a big name. Nvidia’s troubles do not augur well for the rest of the AI complex, making a strong debut for Anthropic more important than ever.”
Singapore’s government has said today it has agreed to continue discussions with the United States about Megaspeed, the company at the centre of the Nvidia scandal.
Singapore’s Minister for Digital Development and Information JosephineTeo discussed Megaspeed with US Deputy Secretary of State ChristopherLandau during a visit to Washington last week, the ministry said in response to a Reuters query, explaining:
“Minister Teo and Deputy Secretary Landau discussed the facts of the case and reaffirmed the commitment by both countries to continuing communications on issues of mutual interest, including on matters relating to Megaspeed.”
Back in the financial markets, the euro has dropped it its lowest level against the US dollar in 18 months.
The euro has dropped to just above $1.1, the weakest since April 2025, as the dollar has rallied against other major currencies.
The euro is on track for its fifth daily fall against the dollar in a row, as investors have anticipated interest rates will rise faster in the US than in the eurozone in coming months.
That’s because inflation is looking particularly sticky in the US.
The German car industry has called on EU leaders to use Friday’s summit with the UK to formally postpone Brexit linked tariffs on exports of electric vehicles into each others territories.
Under the Brexit trade and cooperation agreement levies of 10% on cars and up to 22% on commercial vehicles are due to be imposed on 1 January.
Talks on the tariff are linked to the UK’s demand to be part of the EU’s Made in Europe legislation but that package will not be agreed before 1 January.
The tariffs were originally due to come into force in 2024 but the EU agreed a three year suspension on evidence that neither side had made the expected progress producing their own car batteries.
Under the TCA at least 70% of the battery’s value must have been made in either the UK or the EU to escape the tariff, but industry on both sides of the channel have argued that they have been unable to loosen China’s grip on the rare earths and critical raw materials that make up much of the cost of the battery.
To impose tariffs now would be “putting manufacturers on both sides at a competitive disadvantage” and “would impose new burdens on companies,” said HildegardMüller, president of VerbandderAutomobilindustrie (German Association of the Automotive Industry.)
San Jose Denny's reinstalls plaque honoring former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang
A branch of restaurant chain Denny’s which removed a plaque honoring former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has now decided to bring it back.
The San Jose Denny’s says it is reinstalling the plaque, which was installed in 2023 to highlight the booth where Huang conceived his idea for Nvidia.
As a teenager, Huang’s first job was to wait on tables and wash dishes at a branch of Denny’s, so he and the chain have enjoyed a long connection.
NBC Bay Area reports that the plaque was removed as of Thursday (the day Huang resigned).
Denny’s has now released a statement saying:
“We’re reinstalling the plaque recognizing the conversations at Denny’s that helped launch NVIDIA.
Jensen Huang started at Denny’s as a dishwasher. Years later, he and his co-founders gathered in one of our booths to discuss the idea that became NVIDIA. The plaque commemorates that shared history.
America’s Diner has long been a place where people and ideas come together, and that history deserves to be preserved.”
Shares of Tata Motors Passenger Vehicles have posted their biggest one-day drop in more than four years, after the Indian automaker lowered the margin outlook for its luxury Jaguar Land Rover unit.
On Friday, TataMotors reported a consolidated quarterly net loss of 55.31 billion rupees ($587.7m), weighed down by a one-time charge for employee separation costs tied to JLR’s restructuring and other write-downs.
The carmaker also lowered its full-year adjusted earnings-before-interest-and-tax margin forecast to about 2% to 3% from 4%.
This knocked Tata Motors’ share price down by 8.7% today, the biggest one-day drop since February 2022.
A senior policymaker at the European Central Bank has warned there are growing risks from an “abrupt repricing” in markets and big losses if investor sentiment about artificial intelligence sours.
ECB’s vice president BorisVujcic said the “rapid expansion of AI is creating new challenges for financial stability” in the 21-nation eurozone.
Giving the keynote speech at Euro Finance Week in Frankfurt, Vujcic warned:
“A reassessment of the AI narrative may trigger an abrupt repricing in markets and significant valuation losses.”
Initial public offering volumes relative to US GDP are on track to exceed the levels seen at the height of the dot-com boom of the late 1990s, Vujcic noted, adding:
“Historically, such surges have often coincided with market peaks, pointing to the risk of excessive investor optimism.”
Some European technology stocks are dipping this morning.
SiemensEnergy, which powers AI datacentres, is down 1%, while chipmakers Aixtron (-1.8%) and Infineon (-1.5%) have dropped too.
Vladimir Oleinikov, senior quantitative analyst at Generali Investments, argues that the current correction in valuations is “a valuation reset rather than a structural break”, explaining:
“Concerns around the AI trade have been building since September, as investors increasingly questioned whether unprecedented capex can generate sufficient revenues and free cash flow [FCF].
Since July, hyperscaler revenue forecasts for 2026–28 have risen by $22–235bn, while FCF estimates have fallen by $62–163bn. The November sell-off, amplified by higher yields and wider credit spreads, accelerated this repricing and drove a sharp but temporary spike in volatility (VIX). The Democratic midterm sweep adds regulatory risk to data-centre investment, but presidential and Senate constraints, alongside the US-China AI race, limit the downside. A slower buildout could also ease hyperscaler cash burn and support token pricing.
More recently, the scandal surrounding Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has added another layer of uncertainty, while CoreWeave’s earnings beat last week provides a counterpoint, suggesting that underlying AI demand remains robust.
UK bond yields rise after interest rate rise hints
UK short-term borrowing costs have hit their highest level in in more than two and a half years, after the Bank of England’s chief economist signalled further interest rates are coming.
The yield, or rate of return, on two-year UK gilts have risen over 5% for the first time since February 2024.
Yields rose after the BoE’s HuwPill indicated that the UKK central bank will probably need to raise interest rates next month and again in early 2027 to combat rising inflation.
Pill told the Financial Times: “My view would be, we will see evidence that motivates further rises,” adding that the central bank would “do what is necessary to get inflation back to 2% through time”.
The calls for Jensen Huang to make an (improbable) return as Nvidia’s CEO haven’t brought any sparkle to its share price.
Nvidia’s shares are down almost 2% in premarket trading at $159.67. That’s about 14% below their level just over a week ago, before news broke that Huang had conducted an affair with a suspected Chinese spy.
